analysis.one_liner: Toughens meat, poultry, and egg safety with mandatory pathogen testing, mandatory recalls, and criminal penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Agriculture Committee, and not a single senator signed on to support it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would update the 1907 and 1957 laws governing meat, poultry, and egg inspection. It would declare dangerous bacteria like antibiotic-resistant Salmonella and toxic E. coli strains to be "adulterants" — legal contaminants — so the government could act on them, require large meat and grinding plants to test for these pathogens, give the Agriculture Secretary power to order recalls and post store notices, let the government ban imports from countries that refuse safety audits, add fines of up to $10,000 per violation and prison terms of up to 20 years for knowingly selling unsafe food, protect industry whistleblowers, and commission studies on inspection methods and on meatpacking line speeds and worker safety.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats meat, poultry, or eggs: the bill aims to prevent outbreaks of food poisoning like E. coli and Salmonella, get contaminated product off shelves faster through mandatory recalls and register-posted notices, and trace contamination back to its source. It also protects meat and poultry workers by requiring a study of whether faster processing lines endanger them, and protects employees who report safety problems from being fired.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Meat and poultry consumers; also processing-line workers

how_it_helps.text: Adds antibiotic-resistant Salmonella and dangerous E. coli strains to the legal definition of "adulterated," closing a gap where courts had blocked USDA from treating such bacteria as grounds for action.

Requires slaughterhouses and grinding facilities producing more than 25,000 pounds of trim per day to test for identified pathogens at points in production the Secretary designates, with corrective action required when contaminated product is found.

Gives the Secretary of Agriculture authority to order mandatory recalls when a company will not voluntarily pull contaminated food, and requires grocery stores to post one-page recall notices at cash registers or on the shelf, or call customers who bought recalled items.
Directs USDA to set pathogen-reduction performance standards based on what the best-performing plants already achieve, and lets it ban food imports from countries that refuse onsite safety audits.
Adds civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation and criminal penalties up to 20 years' imprisonment or a $100,000 fine for knowingly introducing unsafe or misbranded food into commerce.
Protects whistleblowers who report food safety violations from being fired, demoted, or harassed, with reinstatement and back pay remedies.

Requires a study of worker safety in meatpacking and poultry processing, including the relationship between line speed and worker safety, and a study of the HACCP-based Inspection Models Project before it is expanded.

analysis.who_pays: Meat, poultry, and egg processors would bear the cost of testing, sampling, record-keeping, corrective action, and potential fines or recalls, and would lose the ability to fight recalls or leave contaminated product in commerce. Grocers would bear small costs posting recall notices. Some compliance costs would likely pass through to food prices.

drawbacks.text: Testing, sampling, and traceability requirements fall on processors, and some of those compliance costs would likely be passed to consumers in food prices.

The initial testing mandate exempts smaller plants (those under 25,000 pounds of daily trim production), so smaller operators get a three-year lead time before the requirement reaches all food establishments.
The citizen-suit provision lets private parties sue both violators and the Secretary for failing to perform non-discretionary duties, which could generate litigation.
The Secretary retains discretion not to prosecute when a civil penalty would "adequately serve the public interest," so the added criminal penalties depend on enforcement priorities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health gain — fewer deaths and illnesses from contaminated meat, faster recalls, and traceable contamination — is the point of the bill, and the main costs are compliance expenses for an industry whose products can sicken or kill consumers when mishandled. The biggest honest caveat is design, not cost: the bill's deadlines layer on each other (surveys, then goals, then standards, then sampling), and its enforcement depends heavily on the Secretary's discretion, so the safeguards are only as strong as the administration carrying them out.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Foodborne Illness Reduction Act of 2011 on September 8, 2011.
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which took no further action on it.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never advanced past committee referral.
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, so the bill died at the end of the session without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat, poultry, and egg processors are better off because the bill died: they avoided pathogen testing mandates, mandatory recall authority, traceability requirements, and new civil and criminal penalties. Consumers gained no additional protections, and the meat and poultry inspection laws the bill targeted remain as the bill described them — last substantially amended decades before.

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its food safety, recall, and worker-safety provisions; served as its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Debbie Stabenow, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 8, 2011 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Every other U.S. senator
against.what_they_did: None of the other 99 senators signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with no bipartisan or even same-party Senate support.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator — including no fellow Democrat — cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have required pathogen testing at their plants, created performance standards benchmarked to their best performers, given the government mandatory recall power, and added criminal penalties for knowingly selling unsafe product. Blocking it preserved the status quo, where USDA's authority over bacteria like Salmonella strains is limited.

industries.industry: Food importers and foreign meat establishments
industries.note: The bill would let USDA remove countries from the import-allowed list if they refuse onsite safety audits or repeatedly fail safety checks, raising the bar for imported meat and poultry. Its defeat keeps the current import regime in place.

The bill would create a laboratory accreditation program and require plant testing to be done by accredited labs, generating new demand for food-testing services. It never became law, so this market was not created.

Stores would have to post recall notices at registers or on shelves and, where they track customer purchases, notify buyers of recalled food — a modest compliance cost aimed at getting contaminated product out of consumers' kitchens faster.
